subject: Accounting
title: The Accrual Principle
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Accrual Principle.

hook.text: You delivered the product in December but got paid in January. When did you earn the revenue?

buildup.text: Cash accounting counts money when it moves. Accrual counts it when it's earned.

discovery.text: Under accrual, revenue is recorded when earned—regardless of when cash arrives.

twist.text: A business can show huge profits on paper while its bank account sits nearly empty.

climax.text: Most large companies use accrual because it paints a more accurate financial picture.

punchline.text: Accrual counts what happened, not just what hit the bank.

quiz.question: Under accrual accounting, when is revenue recorded?

details.summary: The accrual principle records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash is exchanged. It's the foundation of modern accounting and what distinguishes accrual accounting from simple cash-basis tracking.
details.whyItMatters: Accrual accounting gives a more accurate picture of financial performance by matching economic activity to the correct time period rather than tracking only cash movements.
takeaways: Revenue is recorded when the earning process is complete, not when payment is received
Expenses are recorded when the benefit is consumed, not when the bill is paid
GAAP requires accrual accounting for all but the smallest businesses

faq.question: What is the difference between accrual and cash-basis accounting?
faq.answer: Accrual accounting records transactions when they occur economically—revenue when earned, expenses when incurred. Cash-basis records only when cash changes hands. A sale on credit is revenue immediately under accrual but not until payment is received under cash basis.

faq.question: Why is accrual accounting required by GAAP?
faq.answer: Because it provides a more complete and accurate picture of financial performance. Cash-basis accounting can be misleading—a company could delay paying bills to look profitable, or defer invoicing to reduce taxable income. Accrual captures the full economic reality of each period.
